4759:
I paid $375.00 for my first "Personal Computer" unit in November 1981.
I think it had a list price of $399.99 and it was on sale.

They were being sold exclusively by Montgomery Wards.
My Bally's case was white in color and the smokey top had 
"Montgomery Ward" heat stamped in gold on the front.

The 300 baud cassette tape interface with "Bally Basic" cost $99.99 .

The game cassettes were $49.99 on average.

The "Wards" regional Manager here, gave me 3 Astrocade Kiosks when 
they quit selling them. I sold two and kept one, having added casters
 to the base so that it could be easily move around.

The Kiosk has an electronic expansion box inside which is plugged
into the Astrocades expansion port on the rear. This prevented the
game cassettes from being stolen while allowing potential buyers
a chance to try the unit out.

The expansion box holds 7 games in separate slots.

Games are selected by a simple keypad on the left of the arcade unit.
The keypad enables a "Timer" mode to prevent someone entertaining
themselves too long. (AKA "Attract Mode.")
I kept one of these expansion units from one of the Kiosks I sold.

To answer an earlier question as to the capacity of the BLUE RAM
unit that I submitted pictures of....It is 16KB.

Well, it looks like I've finally got a bit of time to work on scanning
stuff.  In case Adam's looking for something to do today, I'll go
ahead and get started with uploads of boxes for Esoterica tape games.

It seems that Esoterica had at least two styles of boxes.  All the
ones on-line so far are color and made out of one piece of cardboard
folded together.  Some of the boxes Mike White sent me don't have
color (except for being a little brownish) and have a separate top and
bottom piece that fit together.  The Great American Jigsaw was
definitely released with both versions.  I believe some of the others
also had new versions because newsletter advertisements had artwork
for them that looks like the new style.  Anyway, here's what we have:

Old Style:

1.  Great American Jigsaw (also has Big City Slick)
2.  Wildcatter (also has Bomb Squad)
3.  Star Trek (also has Mini Golf)
4.  Treasure Island (also has Fox & Hounds)

New Style:

1.  Garbersville (also has Ten Pins)
2.  Hangman (also has Home Budget Keeper) -- This is a 300 dpi rescan
of my box.  I compared the two and this does actually better pick up
fine details like the stripes in the hanged man's tie and the diagonal
lines on the window.

The Hangman scan came out a little crooked, probably from how I was
trying to get the sides into the scan.  Can you straighten these out
easily, Adam?  I'm hoping to hold onto this stuff until it's all
on-line, so I can redo scans if needed.

I'm also including the old scans of my Bally BASIC manual that show
the keypad overlay holder, as discussed earlier.

Look for more stuff soon!  I actually just got a new scanner (Epson
Perfection 44900) that I need to try out.  I've already made some
other scans with an old HP ScanJet 6300C.  So, I'll be interested to
see if anyone can tell the scans apart on the next upload.

Paul
4761:
So, I tried out the new scanner today, and it's almost great.  The
software has a lot of options, and the quality is good.  I found that
using the descreening option on an instruction booklet smoothed the
output enough to look visually closer to the original.  But there's
one facet that's driving me crazy--the scanning software Epson
included doesn't support saving to PNG!  And now that I've realized
how much space I can save with PNG, it's hard to go back.  There's
supposedly a compressed TIFF option in the software, but it seriously
didn't help at all.  So, a 300dpi color scan is 25.5MB.  I used GIMP
to save an image as PNG with maximum compression, and it got down to
5.29MB!  Keep in mind, this is lossless.

Does anyone know of software that will work with the scanner (Epson
Perfection 4490 Photo) to save as PNG?  I can actually do it through
Windows' built-in scanner interface, but it doesn't have nearly as
many options.  Alternatively, I could find a quick way to convert
files to PNG.  A quick Google search found several batch converters,
so I might start experimenting.  Using GIMP wasn't too bad (and
reduced a whole booklet from 55.4MB to 12MB), but I had to convert
each image individually.

Paul

As promised, I've got a big upload coming up.  To go along with the
Bally version instructions now on-line, here are some Astrovision
version instructions.  I took the best sources from my instructions
and the ones Mike White sent me, and now we've got a good upgrade to
our collection.  Here's the rundown.

1.  Artillery Duel
2.  Bally Pin
3.  Biorhythm
4.  Brickyard/Clowns
5.  280 Zzzap/Dodgem
6.  Dog Patch
7.  Grand Prix/Demolition Derby
8.  Pirate's Chase
9.  Solar Conqueror
10. Tornado Baseball/Tennis/Handball/Hockey
11. Galactic Invasion (version 2) -- This is a little strange, but
while this manual that Mike sent me seems to have the same design as
the one now on-line, the front artwork has a definite blue cast while
the one now on-line has a definite purple cast.  It seems like too
much to be from just fading or differences in scanning.  Perhaps
they're from different printings with different inks or something.
It's a mildly interesting variation, I suppose.
12. Galactic Invasion (version 3) -- This is definitely a unique
version of the manual, since it says 'Astrocade' instead of 'Bally' on
the front cover.  And the colors are once again distinct, with the
game artwork using a much lighter blue.
13. AstroBASIC Color Scans -- These are from the same version of the
AstroBASIC manual now on-line, but I made new scans of the front and
back covers (which are now low resolution) and a couple of inside
pages with color (which are now black and white).
14. Astrocade BASIC -- This is the alternate AstroBASIC manual that
says 'Astrocade' instead of 'Bally' on the front cover, and has
various revisions.  I know Adam wasn't really excited about yet
another BASIC manual version, but I wanted to go ahead and scan it
while I had everything out.  And since I probably won't have time to
upload more stuff until after the Thanksgiving holiday, maybe he'll be
looking for something to do.  :-)

Paul

I've been doing tons of research over the past few years for my book and
have a large personal collection, in addition to tons of relevant books and
magazines, and I can say with almost 100% certainty that the computer was
never released in the US (and the fact that Web searches don't even show up
foreign sites leads me to believe it never made it out anywhere in quantity
period).  There were actually quite a few computers introduced in the late
'82 - early '84 timeframe that never made it here.  Most famous is the
distinct lack of any MSX computers, save for the music market-targeted
Yamaha CX5M.  
 
Looking at the Rabbit's supposed specs and other information in that scan
you have, it looks like a bad hybrid of Timex Sinclair 1000/ZX81, Panasonic
JR-200U and Mattel Aquarius, a combination that even in late 1983 at $99
would have been immediately doomed to failure.  It wouldn't really be until
1984 that the C-64 totally came to dominate the low end market in the US
with aggressive price cuts that the competition couldn't match, but with the
bottom falling out of the market already in 1983 and companies like Timex
and Texas Instruments soon to call it quits, it was probably clear to most
companies that there was no way to even get into the market anymore.

Goldfish Demo 1.0

I managed to re-type and assemble Goldfish Demo by Andy Guevara.  This program is dated March 15, 1982.  It is 979 bytes long.

Goldfish Demo won't run unless it is loaded from tape into Machine Language Manager cartridge.  Currently there is no taped version.  The program is meant to reside at memory location $4B40.  It will NOT assemble and run as a cartridge.

Here are the differences between the original source-code and the text version that can be assembled using Zmac:

Version 1.0 (Dec. 11, 2007)

- Program first re-typed from source-code provided by listing discovered in Astrocade lot bought from Larry Anderson.  The lot contains much of the printed material that was owned by Robert Fabris, the publisher of 'The Arcadian' newsletter.

- All program lines correspond to the original program.

- Changed these lines to match syntax of ZMac:
     35  - SPACE can't be used as an equate because Zmac uses it as a pseudo-op.  Changed SPACE to SPAC

     55  - (YPOS.SHL.8)+XPOS to (YPOS SHL 8)+XPOS

     335 - LT is a reserved word (meaning less than).  Changed LT to LMTTBL (Limit Table).

     473 - SPACE can't be used as an equate because Zmac uses it as a pseudo-op.  Changed SPACE to SPAC

     581 - LT is a reserved word (meaning less than).  Changed LT to LMTTBL (Limit Table).

- Checked this program for typing errors.  Compared the listing of this program against the original listing.  It matches byte for byte.

Converting From Hex to AstroBASIC

In order to check the "300-baud to 2000-baud tape conversion" program I needed to convert from hex to AstroBASIC decimal.  There are some AstroBASIC programs to do this, but my Astrocade isn't set up right now.  Here's the way it is done by hand in case anyone wants to do it:

1) Take two hex pairs from a ML program.  Reverse them.  We will use the first two digits of the source-code for the 300-baud to 2000-baud program.  Example: $F3AF = $AFF3

2) Convert the hex to decimal (I use the build-in Windows calculator).  Example: $AFF3 = 45,043

3) If the result is NOT over 32,767, then this number can be entered directly into AstroBASIC.  In our case, the number IS over the limit.

4) If the result IS over 32,767 (as in our example), then subtract 65,636.  The resulting number can be entered into AstroBASIC.  Example: 45,043 - 65,636 = -20493.  Notice that this is the first line to enter into the array when building the 300-to-2000-baud conversion program.

To go from AstroBASIC decimal to hex, just reverse these directions.  For more detailed information on this process see the "Peek 'n Poke" manual on Ballyalley.com:

http://tinyurl.com/3dnonn

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/peek-n-poke-manual-1-21.PDF

This is a useful tid-bit to know-- it also shows how much work was required to program in machine language using Bally or Astro BASIC.  I'm building up a sweat just thinking about it!

Here's a solution for anyone with a memory expansion:

Try thinking like a Basicart designer. Put a routine at !3000 that
jumps to from !2000 of MLM that uses on board subroutine #95 (MOVE)
that copies the !2000 to !3FFF area to !6000 through !7FFF, that
includes a "swap loop" addressed to run somewhere in the !7000 area.
Then lock the expansion into the 6K ROM mode and switch to AB. Load
your work tape into AB as the routine in the MLM book says, call
the "swap loop" and change ranges to 2K. You are now in the MLM with
your work in progress. To save, call the "swap loop" and change
ranges to 6K (stay in ROM mode for both operations, only using RAM
mode to reload MLM to extended memory). You will be in AB ready to
use the interface. The cartridge swapping is eliminated.

Mike W.

General History and Background of Astrocade, Inc.


I.  About this Paper

     This general history is from the Astrocade, Inc. bankruptcy plans filed on February 10, 1984 in Southern District of Ohio, Eastern Division.  The case number is 2-82-04677.  

II.  General History and Background

     The company was incorporated in the State of Delaware on July 3, 1980 as Astrovision, Inc.  By Certificate of Amendment filed April 2, 1982 the company changed its name to Astrocade, Inc. to avoid confusion with other companies using names similar to Astrovision.  The Company was formed by Raymond George together with a small investment group organized primarily by James H. Guerin for the purpose of acquiring the rights to manufacture and market the Bally Arcade Video Game and Home Computer System.  On August 15, 1980 an agreement was entered into between the company and Bally Manufacturing Corporation whereby the company acquired from Bally a five year worldwide exclusive license to certain domestic and foreign patents, patent applications, and inventions enabling the company to practice the technology, manufacture, and sell video game and home computer systems derived from the Bally Arcade.  The company also acquired in that Agreement various component parts inventory, finished goods, test equipment, tooling, and other assets directly related to the Bally Arcade.  Although the company also acquired the right to use the "Bally" trademark, that right expired on December 31, 1981 and is no longer available to the company.  As consideration the company paid Bally approximately One Million Six Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($1,650,000.00) during 1980, 1981, and 1982 plus royalties based upon product sales.  The company's obligation to Bally Manufacturing Corporation for the continued enjoyment of the Agreement includes the payment of past due royalties for the fourth quarter 1982 in the approximate amount of Twenty-five Thousand Dollars ($25,000.00) plus royalties of three percent (3%) of all net sales of product until August 15, 1985.  At that time, the company retains a paid up nonexclusive right and license in the patents, patent applications, and inventions to continue the practice of the technology.
     The product consists of a programmable home video game and micro computer system operated in conjunction with a television set.  The arcade includes a 24-position keyboard that may also be used as a five function ten digit memory calculator, three built in video games, and two eight-way hand held controls.  The arcade offers four player positions and the company markets additional hand controls as an accessory.  The arcade has the capacity to display 256 color variations and is equipped with sound effects generated by a three-channel music synthesizer and sound generator.  A Z-80 Micro-processor provides built in memory of 12,000 bytes.  The use of the custom chip set originally developed by Bally and the configuration of the hand controls has given the arcade industry wide recognition for its technological level.  Continued research and development has led to improvements and refinements in the original arcade and the company believes the arcade remains competitive on a technological level with similarly priced products in the industry.
     The company also markets a BASIC cartridge which allows the operation of the Arcade as a home computer with a variety of educational and creative applications.  The BASIC cartridge is a self-teaching computer programming cartridge which has a built in audio interphase system permitting the permanent storage of consumer created programs on cassette tapes.
     The company currently offers approximately 36 video games including space, adventure, sports, strategy, action and skill, and educational programs.  With the exception of the three games built into the Arcade the remaining games are offered as accessories in preprogrammed cassettes.
     The company is also researching the development of a Z-Grass system which would permit the use of the arcade as a home computer with a full range of typical home computer applications.  The Z-Grass system would include a 60-key typewriter style keyboard and an additional 100,000 bytes of memory (64K-RAM, 32K-ROM and 4K SCREEN-RAM).  The Z-Grass system would permit standard interfacing with a variety of peripheral accessories designed and offered by independent vendors including compatibility with most standard floppy disc systems. Although final determination cannot be made until the development research is completed, management believes that the arcade and Z-Grass system can be offered at a competitive price with other combination video game and home computer systems.
     Until March, 1982 the company purchased its own component parts inventory and subcontracted the assembly of the arcade to E. F. Johnson Company and Sierratronics, Inc.  The cost of maintaining the component parts inventory was a substantial burden on the company and in June, 1982 the company sold its component parts inventory to Nitron, Inc.  From that time on it was anticipated that Nitron, Inc. would purchase component parts inventory on its own account and handle the manufacturing of the arcade as well as software cassettes.  The new subcontract for manufacturing with Nitron, Inc. was also designed to cure certain quality control problems which the company had experienced previously as a result of not having quality control personnel on site at the assembly operation.  As a result of Astrocade's inability to pay Nitron, Inc. due to the company's financial condition combined with the financial condition of Nitron the production of product during the last half of 1982 was sporadic and there was no continuing production of new product at the time of the commencement of the Chapter 11 proceeding.  After the filing of the Chapter 11 proceeding arrangements were made for the production of limited quantities of software to fill various orders.  With the exception of the custom silicon data chip set which is currently obtainable only from a single source, multiple sources of supply are available for virtually all of the materials and components comprising the company's products.
     The company's products are presently serviced by E. F. Johnson Company at its facility in Garner, Iowa.  The Plan provides that the company will continue to honor the standard warranty given with each product sold with respect to both pre-petition and post-petition sales to the end consumer.  Subsequent to confirmation the Debtor may use a different facility for warranty and repair service.  The company's warranty program provides an over-the-counter exchange during 90 days following purchase.  These products are returned by the retail seller to be repaired and placed in new and saleable condition.  In addition, consumers return products outside the 90 day warranty period and pay a flat fee for repairs.  Historically, the fees paid by consumers have been sufficient to support the repair not only of the out-of-warranty but also the in-warranty products.
     The company distributes products through several channels of distribution including direct sales to in-house accounts and a network of representatives and distributors.  The company's largest single account has been Montgomery Ward which comprised approximately one-third of the company's total sales since its formation.
     During 1982 the rate of growth in the industry slowed from its tremendous growth during 1981.  Notwithstanding the slower rate of growth the industry volume was up an estimated 90% from 1981.  Industry analysts generally believe this growth trend will continue but at somewhat slower rates of increase.  Notwithstanding the rapid growth in the industry during the last several years, estimated penetration of the United States television households was estimated at about 18% at year end 1982.  During 1982 the industry experienced overstocking of inventory, and in particular software games.  The industry also was entered by a number of software companies producing large volumes of relatively low quality games.  The introduction in the second half of 1982 of the ColecoVision System demonstrated to many market analysts, however, the continuing viability in the industry of systems with high resolution, good graphics, and quality software.  At year end 1982 the saturation of the foreign market was only estimated to be approximately 3% making this market significant for the future of the industry.
     The management of the debtor believes that the Astrocade system and games compete on a technological level with the quality of systems and games offered by the chief competitors during 1982, however, such competitors control the vast majority of the market share.  The debtor is not anticipated to have the necessary resources to compete for any significant market share.  Although Atari, the industry leader, enjoyed an increase in both console and game sales in 1982 from 1981, Atari's market share was eroded by the introduction of the ColecoVision system and the market share of software games was eroded by the introduction of independent manufacturers of Atari compatible games.
     The sales of the debtor for the year ending December 31, 1981 were approximately 9.4 million dollars net of discounts, returns and allowances.  Although sales at year end 1982 increased to approximately 11.2 million dollars net of discounts, returns and allowances, approximately 4 million dollars of such sales are the subject of pending disputes.  Due to the cash flow problems of the debtor and the traditionally slow market period during the first half of the calendar year following the Christmas season, the debtor's sales since the filing of the Chapter 11 petition have been negligible.  Management believes, however, that sales levels can be restored to previous levels with a steady growth rate with the introduction of the product into foreign markets.  The debtor has completed the research and development necessary to manufacture the console to be compatible with both the NTSC television format used in the United States and portions of Asia and the PAL television format used in most of Europe.  Marketing of the console in Europe requires the finalization, however, of a 50 Hertz Data Chip so that the console will provide full screen display on older European televisions.  Management presently believes the 50 Hertz Data Chip can be finished at a cost of approximately $30,000.00.
     During 1981 the company had continuing cash flow difficulties due primarily from the costs of acquiring and maintaining component parts inventory for the manufacture of the console.  The continued expense of supporting the manufacturing process led the company, however, at year end 1981 to seek additional sources of capital.  These efforts resulted in an agreement entered into in approximately February, 1982 between the original investor group and Roger Greenman in which Mr. Greenman, among other things assumed the role of Chief Operating Officer and Chief Executive Officer and obtained the right to acquire controlling stock in the company.  Continued efforts to raise capital led to an agreement (the effect and validity of which is subject to dispute) entered into in May, 1982 with Quaker Oats Company.  Quaker Oats Company, the parent of Fisher Price Toys purchased one million shares of the debtor's stock for the cash price of $3,000,000.00.  Pursuant to the terms of the agreement Quaker Oats exercised its option to rescind the stock purchase and convert the three million dollar infusion of funds to debt, all of which was to be repaid during 1982.
     At the outset of 1982 the company's right to use the Bally trademark expired and the company planned to market its products under its corporate name of Astrovision.  After incurring substantial advertising and promotional expenses to introduce the Astrovision name, it became apparent that the confusion and conflicting claim of rights to that name prevented its use by the company.  Thereupon, the Astrocade name was selected.  This caused an unfortunate duplication in the expense of gaining market recognition.  The company paid through direct media and cooperative advertising approximately 3.5 million dollars in 1982 and incurred a roughly similar amount which remained unpaid at the filing of the Chapter 11 petition.
     The extensive advertising and promotion expense of gaining market recognition under the name Astrocade, and the interruption in manufacturing resulting from cash flow problems of the company and Nitron, Inc. were all significant factors leading to the filing of the Chapter 11 petition.
     Many of the pre-petition transactions of the Debtor are discussed and additional financial analysis of the Debtor is contained in the preliminary report of the Court appointed Examiner, Ernst & Whinney.  This report is available at the Court for inspection by parties in interest.

Adam, Goldfish Demo by The Bit Fiddlers.  This is available in a
variety of formats.  One side is the MLM version, which can be loaded
into Machine Language Manager through the 300 baud interface.  Adam
typed in these directions, which seemed like nonsense the first time I
read them, but then made perfect sense once I started up the MLM
cartridge and looked at the overlay.

; Hit RESET
; Hit CALL
; Enter B then WRITE for # of text lines
; Enter four WRITES
; Type * READ
; Start Recorder
; When done loading
; Type **4B40 CALL

Actually, you only have to enter three WRITES after entering B WRITE
(so there are four WRITES in total).  When entering time, use the
numbering from the calculator keypad (different from BASIC numbering).

The other side of the tape has the BASIC version in both 300 baud and
2000 baud format.  These should be loaded with :RUN, and also use the
calculator numbering.

All versions are essentially the same.  Seven goldfish swim around
independently, a clock runs, and the cat meows every minute.  Check it
out!

pages being skewed, don't blame me this time; they were actually

If you use the HVGLIB (Home Video Game Library) equate header file, then your source code will be a bit more natural.  The header file is available here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/HVGLIB.zip

This header is intended to work with the Zmac assembler, which is what we've been using for Astrocade homebrew programming.  The Windows command line version of the cross-assembler is available here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/Zmac13_win32.zip

There is also a compiled Linux version available.

Using the header file, you could have source-code that looks like this:

INCLUDE HVGLIB.H

	SYSSUK	PAWS		;PAUSE FOR
	DB  	1		;ONE CYCLE

Since you're using PAWS, you obviously know about the Nutting manual.  The manual and the header file go hand and hand.  Since you're using a different assembler, you may have to modify the header file slightly, as it makes extensive use of macros.

Adam Trionfo was sorta happily shocked that my former interest in old
video games and/or hardware has sort of mildly been rekindled ... and
he was even happier when I said I'd go online ...

Astrocade multi-carts I once designed and manufactured (entirely by
hand) are still somewhere high on many Bally fan's popularity lists.

Anyway ... Adam's been a good friend of mine for years. For no huge 
reason other than it felt like the right thing to do, earlier today I
sent some things to him that (assuming nothing goes wrong to prevent
it from happening?), may make some of you rather happy campers!?

I sent Adam the computer files I used, to print out photo-etching
masks, for both sides of my multi-cart's printed circuit board; along
with some text info (mainly, my old cheatsheat of what order to hook
up the internal jumper wires ... closest thing to written "factory
instructions" I ever used, since I largely just copied examples of
the first carts I did, when I hand-wired later ones); and finally two
high-res scans of cart innards -- fully assembled and "ready to go".

In other words, production of my multi-cart design can theoretically
resume ... as soon as someone with enough technical knowledge gets up
enough of a wild hair to volunteer to pick it up, where I left off.

Doing so allows me to stay technically retired, in regards to future
etching or soldering work ... while it cuts the risk down that folks
will endlessly bug me to resume production of my MC's. Which means
I'll get to just hang out again, online; and relax and have fun.

As you'll see when he posts it, I put strike-through lines on any of
the copyright messages that I once had on that photo-mask artwork. I
won't mind if others take my years-old work, and keep going with it.

I figured I'd pass my multi-cart torch. Other folks have given
their "it's okay to use my stuff" nod to fans of this system. (Or at
least that was my memory of it, when I "retired" around 2003. Adam
does very good work, I think, on that sort of thing! Others, too?)

Before anyone hollers, or threatens me with great bodily harm, allow
me to make some relevant points clear:

The hand-drawn, hand-etched boards I made went through 3 revisions: I
think of them as Revisions A, B, and C. I did not send any of that
artwork to Adam. I still have all three, safely stored on my PC (and
backed up on CD-ROMs.) This means that to exactly duplicate what I
did, five or more years ago, would involve re-drawing the board art,
and then also etching and cutting and blah-blah each board by hand.

I suspect it's much more likely, if anyone takes what I'm giving and
runs with it, that they'll drop the hand-drawn artwork into CAD ...

What I did was to take the "C" board style; change a few things on
it -- mostly text, not the actual circuit design -- and gave this new
artwork version a new name: "Revision D". That and some other subtle
differences should help to prevent any future imposters, so to speak.

Just to be sure, I placed "Reproduction --- not an original" in large
bold lettering, on the etch design itself. (In the same spot where my
old e-mail address used to be.) I hope that if anyone re-draws the PC
board pattern I used -- by hand or via computer -- that they also put
some reasonably evident notice that it's a repro or next generation.

If the board artwork I just made public is used "as is," it would
still work in exactly the same way as before, electronically ... but
the back side of each PC board would prominently say "Reproduction".

While I'm not a collector, myself -- and I don't even HAVE one of my
own Bally multi-carts, any more, since I sold my personal one in
2004; and gave the first test one to Adam, in 2005 I think -- I still
wanted to try to protect the collector value of the 43 Bally multi-
carts I once made by hand. Just seemed like the fair thing to do: a
nod of thanks to those buyers who took a chance on a Home Brew Guy.

That should probably put most collector's minds at rest? Hopefully?

If not: note that I did *not* send Adam the print-able label art I
once used ... making it that much harder for unauthorized clones of
the original 43 carts to be made (without detection). Pretty much, it
comes down to this: anyone crazy enough to think they can make $$$ by
cheating well-heeled collectors via a TOTALLY hand-made reproduction,
really has a screw loose! I know better than most, how much work such
things take, so I simply can't see anyone creating precise clones.

So ....

Hopefully, most folks will find this agree-able, and will be glad I
did it? (If not, oh well! Can't please 'em all!) I know a number of
folks have publicly posted, in one place or other, saying they wished
they had known; or had taken the opportunity when it was there? (CGE
2002 being a prime example: MC sales weren't exactly overwhelming at
that time, so I lowered the price to where I was losing even more of
my time/money, on the last ones ... and when my Bally console burned
out, along with my motivation to keep making MC's ... that was that!)

I figure passing on the PCB artwork is sort of a cool curiousity, for
the reader's of Adam's site ... plus it's a way for me to pass on the
Bally multi-cart torch ... without having to do any more hand-
etching / soldering / labeling -- not to mention finding shells! ...
while also doing what I can to keep the previous cart's buyers happy.

  -- Ward Shrake --

Hi all. Way back in 2001, Mike White and I used to talk on the phone
about Bally-related stuff. I have no idea if it's still true, but at
the time Mike told me the existing new-old-stock supply of blank PC
boards was dwindling. I was working on the first multi-carts, around
that time ... enough that I knew they'd work, when we were talking.

At the time, I had volunteered myself to come up with what I felt
would be a good general-purpose Bally cart PC board design, to fit
that need: in other words, a generic "one-size-fits-all" single-cart
design, so he (and/or others) could make single Home-Brew'ed carts.

The major criteria was that it should work with any (reasonable!)
EPROM chip that Mike was likely to want to use; that the boards be as
cheap to manufacture as possible (that being the case, I pushed for
doing it as a singe-sided board; rather than the more expensive
double-sider's); and that it would be set up more for hand-assembly
than machine work. Oh, and it had to fit into his plastic cases.

The one big "trick" (or bit of lateral thinking) would be to bend the
legs of through-board EPROMs; making them imitation "surface mount"
chips. That would eliminate the need for drilling all but three holes
in the board; and the bottom of the board could then simply be blank.

I bring that all up because I just posted a scan of the original
artwork I did for that project, in the FILES >> TEMP folder.  :-)

I'm not sure if that's a project I'm gonna "stay quitted on" or not?
I do still have an interest in old hardware; and I definitely want to
get un-rusty on PC board etching (for totally unrelated projects: I
am into scale models now, and may want to do some lighting for some
of the bigger ones I'm making) ... so I'm thinking that I might want
to at least do a few "test the theory" boards, using that design. If
it worked as well as I'd hoped, I'd probably re-draw it for neatness
and then etch a few more: and either post that artwork and/or follow
through on my original threats to Mike: to send him boards he could
then turn over to a board-making shop, for them to copy the design.

That sounds like it, yeah.  It does not do component.  Component is a high
end connection.  It does coaxial (cable), composite and S-Video (the coaxial
is one dongle, while the composite/s-video is another dongle).  I captured
these screenshots with my unmodified Astrocade:
http://www.flickr.com/photos/loguidice/sets/72157603585712286/.  Obviously
it also captures video just fine as well.  It's hit or miss with what
systems the GameBridge works with as some systems have unusual syncing.  For
instance, the C-64/128, Astrocade and Atari 2600 all work fine, while the
Apple II, Panasonic JR-200U and Timex Sinclair 2068 don't.  For the
Astrocade I used the coaxial connection with a standard F Type adapter
(http://www.atariage.com/store/index.php?main_page=product_info
<http://www.atariage.com/store/index.php?main_page=product_info&products_id=
42> &products_id=42) since I don't use switchboxes on any of my systems.
 
Just a note, while it was designed for Windows XP, it will work just fine
with Windows Vista if you install it in a compatible manner (it works fine
on my Windows Vista Tablet PC, which is what I always use for captures these
days).  Also, capturing audio/video takes a lot of resources, so you may
have to assign a higher priority to the task when the application is
running.  This way you get full frame/full speed captures, which are
actually quite nice.  Obviously for screenshots you don't need to prioritize
the running instance.
